title: Taxes
question: Who should pay taxes in the United States, and what should those taxes be for?
summary: Who pays, what the money funds, and why people use the word “fair” to mean different things.
sourceNote: Further reading only. This outline does not take facts from these pages yet. When the full page is written, government or other primary sources will be cited first, and the Just Facts page will stay linked as further reading. The wording on this site will stay original. No statistics are included here.

paragraphs: This section will explain the main kinds of U.S. taxes in everyday words: taxes on pay, taxes on what people buy, and taxes on what people and companies earn. It will say what those taxes are used for, without a pile of dollar figures until the figures are checked.
No statistics will be added until they are checked against primary sources.

This section will name the real disagreement about fairness. Some people think a fair tax takes a larger share from people with more money. Others think a fair tax takes the same share, or that lower taxes on work and investment help everyone by growing the economy. The page will steel-man both ideas.

sides.intro: Each column will hold one side’s strongest fair case, in plain language and at similar length. Neither case is written yet.

a.title: One side’s strongest case
paragraphs: This column will give the strongest fair case for one view, using checked facts. It will not use insults, and it is not written yet.

b.title: The other side’s strongest case
paragraphs: This column will give the strongest fair case for the other view, under the same rules. It is not written yet.
This section will look for points that do not require picking a tax plan first, such as wanting the rules to be understandable and wanting the government to say clearly what the money buys.

items: The questions will ask what “fair” should mean, who feels a tax even when someone else writes the check, and how a person can tell a hope about the economy from a fact.
